title: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We may in all probability ascribe to this fact and to its converse, or at least associate with it, such phenomena as the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter, or the frequent formation of strong shells or membranous capsules in “winter-eggs.”

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VI, “A Note on Adsorption”; topic “Encystment and surface tension”. Scope: encysting protists and invertebrates producing winter or resting eggs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch06-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Temperature and encystment phenology are measurable, but the adsorption mechanism is harder to distinguish from other seasonal cues. Existing records support broad correlational tests rather than a decisive mechanistic resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate temperature histories to encystment or resting-egg shell thickness while controlling photoperiod, nutrition, and season, and test whether colder conditions consistently increase membrane formation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Occurrence records rarely measure adsorption or capsule strength directly.

Season covaries with photoperiod, food, and desiccation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Seasonal encystment and winter-egg formation are documented for rotifers, cladocerans and some protists, so the ecological association can be inspected for a subset. The claimed mechanism, reduced temperature favouring adsorption, is not what those datasets measure. Photoperiod and crowding remain serious alternative drivers, which keeps the test only partly informative.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether encystment and resting-egg shell thickening track falling temperature after photoperiod, crowding and food are accounted for, and whether wall-material adsorption rises as temperature falls. A temperature-specific increase in adsorption and encystment would support the claim; encystment timed by photoperiod at constant temperature would weaken it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Adsorbability of the actual wall molecules versus temperature is laboratory physical chemistry and is not in these environmental archives.

Resting-egg and cyst induction is confounded with photoperiod and resource cues that field temperature series do not separate.
